background.definition: Hypernatremia is defined as a serum sodium concentration greater than 145 mEq/L.

list.listitem: Incidence among hospital admissions: 0.2%.
Incidence of hospital-acquired hypernatremia: 1%.
More common in infants and the elderly.

Among 5179 community-living patients over age 55 years, 15% had at least once electrolyte abnormality; hypernatremia occurred in 3.4%. The use of loop-diuretics was independently associated with hypernatremia; other studies identified the presence of Alzheimer's disease and the use of renin-angiotensin system blockers as risk factors for hypernatremia among patients over age 74 years.
See for causes of hypernatremia.
Sodium is a functionally impermeable solute in the extracellular fluid, which along with extracellular anions (bicarbonate and chloride) accounts for most of the serum osmolality.

The serum sodium concentration reflects the balance between total body water (TBW) and total body sodium. Hypernatremia reflects a deficit of water in relation to total body sodium content. This can result from net water loss (most common cause) or sodium gain.

Water homeostasis is controlled primarily by the "thirst center" in the hypothalamus and AVP, the antidiuretic hormone (ADH). AVP secretion is stimulated by a rise in serum osmolality, which in turn promotes water reabsorption in the distal collecting duct of the nephrons. Thirst is a powerful stimulus for water intake, so hypernatremia almost never develops in alert subjects with access to water.

Newborns should be seen within 3 to 5 days of hospital discharge to ensure adequacy of breast feeding to avoid hypernatremic dehydration. Weight loss more than 7% should raise suspicion for dehydration and hypernatremia. B
Caregivers of nursing home residents should carefully monitor for change in level of consciousness as it is strongly associated with development of hypernatremia. B
Clinical presentation is nonspecific and may include tachypnea, restlessness, or lethargy in infants and altered mental status in the elderly. C
Diagnosis can be established by assessing the hypothalamus-AVP-renal axis; determine serum osmolality, urine osmolality, urine sodium, and serum glucose to establish the diagnosis. C

Symptoms are more prominent when the increase in serum sodium is large or occurs rapidly. Acute hypernatremia could cause vascular rupture in the brain (intracerebral or subarachnoid) by shear stress induced by cell shrinkage. Chronic hypernatremia tends to be relatively asymptomatic until the sodium level is very high.

Most patients with hypernatremia are either very young or very old. Infants can present with tachypnea and restlessness interspersed with lethargy. Presentation in the elderly tends to be nonspecific. Change in the level of consciousness, though nonspecific, was strongly associated with development of hypernatremia.
Patients with diabetes insipidus tend to present with polyuria and polydipsia.
Patients with hypernatremia resulting from hypotonic fluid loss could present with decreased skin turgor, decreased jugular venous pressure (JVP), tachycardia, and hypotension.
Physical examination should focus on evaluation of volume status (skin turgor, JVP, and orthostatic blood pressures) and neurological status.

If serum sodium is elevated, determine serum osmolality and obtain a serum glucose to assess osmotic diuresis as possible etiology. Serum osmolality is determined by the concentrations of different solutes in the plasma. In normal subjects, sodium, glucose, and urea are the primary circulating solutes.

The next step is evaluation of the hypothalamic-AVP-renal axis by measuring urine osmolality. Hypernatremia leads to increased serum osmolality, which is a very potent stimulus for AVP secretion, which in turn leads to excretion of a minimal amount of maximally concentrated urine.

If urine osmolality is elevated, both hypothalamic and renal functions are intact. Urine osmolality is decreased in central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (typically less than 300 mOsm/L); it is increased in hypertonic sodium gain and extrarenal fluid losses (typically more than 700 mOsm/L). Intermediate values could be from renal fluid losses (eg, osmotic diuresis).
Urine sodium is useful to differentiate renal (urine sodium is increased) and extrarenal (urine sodium is decreased) hypotonic fluid losses.
Obtain a water-restriction test when diabetes insipidus is suspected.
Consider CT scan of the brain in severely hypernatremic patients or hypernatremic patients presenting with altered mental status to rule out intracranial bleeding.
Serum osmolality can be estimated using the following equation: Serum osmolality = (2 x Na) + (BUN/2.8) + (Glucose/18) + (Ethanol/4.6).

Treatment should be focused on treating the possible etiology, correction of hypernatremia, and avoiding complications of rapid correction. C
Initial fluid of choice is based on the volume status and the presumed etiology of hypernatremia. C
Treatment goals are to correct hypernatremia and to avoid complications from rapid correction. Initial fluid choice is based on the volume status (skin turgor, JVP, and orthostatic blood pressures).
If hypovolemic and hypotensive, use isotonic fluids (0.9% saline). Once hemodynamically stable, use hypotonic fluids.
If hypovolemic and hemodynamically stable, use hypotonic fluids (0.45% saline, 0.2% saline).
If euvolemic, the preferred route of water replacement is oral. Intravenous fluids (5% dextrose in water) could also be used.
If hypervolemic, the treatment is a combination of loop diuretics and free water replacement with 5% dextrose in water.

Treatment complications such as cerebral edema and seizures result from too rapid correction of the hypernatremia. Therefore, sodium concentration should not be lowered at >0.5 mEq/L per hour and no more than 12 mEq/L per day.

Several formulae () are available to assist in the calculation of free water deficit and to estimate the effect of 1 L of IVFs. However, the formulae rely on TBW, and the clinical estimates of TBW are rather crude, so frequent measurements of serum Na must be performed in concert with whichever calculation is used.

Rapid-onset, acute hypernatremia caused by sodium overload due to ingestion or iatrogenically is rare. Case reports describe treatment using rapid infusion of dextrose-based solutions, with 13 of 18 survivors in these reports having relatively rapid reduction in sodium (less than 146 meq/L within 48 hours).
Significant mortality rate, ranging from 42% to 60%, reported in adults. B
Fifteen percent to 20% mortality rate in children; followup needed for neurological sequelae. C

In critically ill neurologic or neurosurgical patients, hypernatremia (serum sodium >150 mmol/l) occurs in 5% of patients (vs. 17% with hyponatremia), and was a significant predictor of mortality (OR = 5.3).

Additionally, among 20,029 patients with preoperative hypernatremia (defined as >144 mmol/L), the 30-day mortality rate was 5.2%. Perioperative major coronary events (1.6% vs. 0.7%), pneumonia (3.4% vs. 1.5%) and venous thromboembolism (1.8% vs. 0.9%) were more common than in a normonatremic cohort.

Defined as serum sodium of >149 mEq/L, ICU acquired hypernatremia develops in 4.3% of patients and is an independent risk factor for longer ICU length of stay (RR 1.28) and higher mortality (RR 1.40).
Have a high clinical suspicion because of the nonspecificity of symptoms in the elderly.
Change in level of consciousness is strongly associated with development of hypernatremia and is an indicator of poor prognosis.

Guidelines from the Royal Children's Hospital in Melbourne, Australia recommend initiating therapy with IV sodium chloride 0.9% plus glucose 5%. They also recommend that the rate of correction should not be higher than 0.5 mmol/L/hr (10-12 mmol/L/day) to avoid neurologic injury, seizures, and cerebral edema.

The guidelines also recommend that all children have paired serum and using osmolality, but that this measurement should not delay the initiation of therapy. They note that infants and small children are at greater risk for hypernatremia because they cannot always ask for fluids, and also experience greater insensible losses due to a higher ratio of body surface to mass.
